endorsements.quote: In practice, for task-specific diagnostic models, prospective accuracy studies should use adjudicated or probabilistic reference standards and explicitly model of ground-truth uncertainty.

In assistive and ensemble settings, cluster-randomized or stepped-wedge trials can compare human-AI ensembles with unaided clinicians; as well, silent-mode deployments hiding recorded AI outputs from clinicians can reveal discrepancy patterns and drift.
Standardized prospective studies should compare AI-assisted clinicians with those using conventional resources against definitive clinical endpoints, rather than against each other's labels.

unlisted_practices: Validate medical AI against a probabilistic ground truth that captures expert disagreement and uncertainty, using latent-class models or adjudication panels that record uncertainty scores alongside labels.
Treat evaluation of the human reference-standard benchmark itself as a first-class requirement for trustworthy medical AI.
Use outcome-based validation with patient-relevant endpoints such as time to diagnosis, safety, and cost-effectiveness rather than agreement with human labels alone.
Evaluate humans and AI bidirectionally, auditing both against probabilistic ground truth and each other.

Before using AI as a reference layer for auditing human performance, require robust external validation across institutions and populations, calibration and uncertainty estimation, systematic drift monitoring, transparent version control, defined procedures for adjudicating AI-clinician disagreements, evidence of association with clinical outcomes, and regulatory and fairness oversight.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint/commentary discussing the limitations of relying on human ground truth for evaluating AI in medicine, recommending outcome-based validation and evaluating human-AI ensembles.
